title: Unnamed and inline namespaces
recap: Names declared in an unnamed namespace have internal linkage, making an unnamed namespace a convenient home for implementation details that should remain inside one translation unit. Unnamed namespaces generally belong in source files rather than headers.

An inline namespace exposes its members through the enclosing namespace while retaining a qualified version name. This supports a default API version while allowing callers to request an older or alternate version explicitly.
objectives: Keep a pricing implementation detail in a source-file unnamed namespace.
Declare old and current API versions in named namespaces.
Make the current version available through an inline namespace.
Call the default, legacy, and explicitly named current APIs.
warnings: Do not place unnamed namespaces in headers; each including translation unit would receive distinct entities.
Inline namespaces do not give their contents internal linkage.
Only one version should be inline when unqualified access through the parent namespace must be unambiguous.
challenge: Build a versioned Pricing API. V1::total returns the subtotal unchanged. Inline namespace V2::total adds a source-file-only service fee of 3 stored in an unnamed namespace. Print calls through Pricing::V1, the default Pricing namespace, and Pricing::V2 to demonstrate version selection.
hints: Declare namespace V1 normally and prefix namespace V2 with inline in pricing.h.
Put the serviceFee constant in namespace followed directly by an unnamed block in pricing.cpp.
Pricing::total resolves to the member of inline namespace V2.
